Michael Jackson describes the product
of this distillery as `The greatest all-
rounder in the world of malt whisky'.
Try this medium gold nectarate from its
long sleep in a hoggie and you will see
what he means. The nose is slightly elu-
sive at first though we found toffee,
fudge and candy sugar with hazelnuts
and a touch of smoke. When water is
introduced, however, it shows itself to
be a complex and rewarding dram with
orange blossom, beer kegs, porridge
and dampers. The taste is fresh but big
� sweet and briny with orange, choco-
late and malt beer. A real beauty!

"Hot and Honeyed"
This distillery is on Clydebank, near
Old Kilpatrick (Kilpatrick means the
church of St. Patrick, which might ex-
plain why triple distillation, normally
associated with Irish whiskeys, is still
practiced here). From a , this
dram is the 
The nose is sharp and complex, with
lemon butter puffs and pear at the end
and cedar cigar boxes at the other. Wa-
ter brings out lemon, almonds and
string mop heads. It is mellifluous and
can take plenty of water.

product_name: Chocolates and a Bunch of Flowers
tasting_notes_raw:
"Chocolates and a Bunch of Flowers"
The distillery, which continues the
Lowland tradition, lies on the very edge
of Glasgow. Morrison Bowmore took it
over the same year this American bar-
rel was filled. The 
copper gold and the nose carries a mes-
sage of chocolates and bunches of flow-
ers, butterscotch and peaches and
cream. Water freshens it up slightly.
The taste is quite distinctive, with syr-
upy sweetness, nicely balanced by
something related to Sambuca and
some even more exotic flavours of rose
petals and lychees. A very interesting
and rewarding whisky.

Lowlands, Western Lowlands
 Pineapples dipped in honey
With Gummy Bears, vanilla baked apples, mari-
nated cherries, carrot cake with orange icing,
wet wood, cough syrup and beeswax this was
a warming and inviting nose. The palate did-
n't disappoint with tastes of orange, fudge,
beeswax polish, honeycomb and black pepper.
Water really opened everything up and
brought forth aromas of orange blossom, lolly
pop sticks, orange flavoured Calippo ice
lollies, mixed dried herbs, plums and baked
apples, vanilla and pineapples in honey. On the
palate it was sweet, spicy, thickly mouth
coating and oily with tastes of black pepper,
liquorice root and root ginger. From the low-
land distillery that triple distils.

Lowlands, Western Lowlands
 A charming evocation of summer
The nose was a fresh and charming evocation
of summer � apple pie, cinnamon, rhubarb and
custard, pineapple juice, lime, papaya, pear
and banana. To taste, we found it a sweet and
citric mix � lemon curd on digestive biscuits,
sherbet lemons, grape skins, flying saucers,
etc. � but along with that, some varnished pine
and green beans. The reduced nose was
very pleasant, with light vegetable oil, cider
or perry, cranberry juice, icing sugar and a
forest glade with boulders, after the rain. The re-
duced palate found Empire biscuits and pleas-
ant creamy textures � exceedingly drinkable.
From a distillery just west of Glasgow.

Lowlands, Western Lowlands
 Laundry in the Bakery
Initial nose is fresh and light, elderflower cor-
dial, green apples and lemon puffs. Deeper
and sweeter notes develop quickly, giving
homely and warm feeling, like baking bread or
jam doughnuts. Quite hot and lively to taste,
strawberries with black pepper, turning
fruity and fizzy like strawberry Creamola foam,
also creamy similar to a raspberry milk shake or
Macchiato coffee. That creaminess carries on
when adding water and aromas of apple
toffee, rice pudding, butter icing, straw-
berry jam and doughy bread emerge. The
taste is that of dark hot chocolate, brown sugar,
cinnamon and blackberry jam. And to fin-
ish, from this distillery known for distilling
three times, cold peppermint tea and fresh slightly
soapy laundry.

Lowland
Rubbing White Tiger Balm on your forehead
 We were greeted by a wonderfully fresh
 aroma like a menthol and eucalyptus inhalation
 or the smell of a small amount of Tiger
 Balm White rubbed into our foreheads. We
 carried on very relaxed and discovered baked
 plums, bananas on burnt toast and peppered
 oat cakes. The taste was fresh and juicy
 like very ripe strawberries with a sprinkling of
 pepper and a deeper note of mace essential oil
 blended with coriander. Adding water we
 found ourselves in an old barn making arti-
 san French cider, eating classic Greek Feta cheese
 and drinking a hoppy German Pilsner. The
 taste now is sweet like pineapple syrup and
 as juicy as a pink grapefruit.

Lowland
 Lemon drizzle cake
Tart apple pie, with grass clippings, lemon zest/lemon
marmalade, key lime pie and a hint of sherbet.
Surprisingly sweet in the mouth, with lime,
lemon sherbet then strawberry jello and wine gums.
Water reinforces this with boiled sweets and
artificial red fruits; fresh bread or proving dough
and cornflakes behind. Not as sweet now, but
soft and fruity (tinned fruit cocktail); mouth-cooling,
with a short finish. Fresh and easy to drink,
with a trace of lemon-grass in the after-
taste. An excellent aperitif.

Lowland
 Soft, Sweet and Fluffy
The initial impression was one of delicate
sweetness, soft and elegant like baby lotion and
talcum powder. This was followed by sweet
lemonade, sweet coconut milk, hazelnuts, cof-
fee and chocolate ice cream and the hint of
a perfume/floral aroma, possibly hydran-
gea. Super sweet on the palate neat but then
at the same time an intriguing spiciness of cin-
namon and nutmeg. The finish had an ever
so slightly bitter and tangy hoppy flavour like
in a chocolate stout. Water made it feel like
crawling into a fluffy onesie at the end of a
long day with sweet waffles and a hot chocolate
by your side.

product_name: SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
tasting_notes_raw:
SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
 FLORAL PERFUMES IN A CHINESE
 R E S TA U R A N T
We found the nose straightforward but attractive, with vanilla, lemon puffs, green
apple, rhubarb and chalky sweets (Edinburgh Rock) but one panellist was in a
Chinese restaurant (five-spice, fragrant rice, fortune cookies). With water the floral,
citric perfumes edged forward and it became more buttery (popcorn, shortbread,
caramel). The palate had good viscosity and body, with sweet and tart flavours of
stewed rhubarb, gooseberry, plums, red grape Shloer, Haribos and Astro Belts; it
even seemed fizzy and lively at times. Water emphasised different aspects �
pistachios, almonds and salty bread, with lemon rind, white pepper and aniseed
bringing dryness to the finish.

DEEP, RICH & DRIED FRUITS
 STAVE NEW WORLD
 The wood hit our noses as oak shavings, fresh-cut pine and furniture stores;
 then we detected eucalyptus, ginger and new leather shoes; but it was also
 sweet (Oreos, syrup, plum sauce on sponge) and floral. The palate's deeper
 regions gave us liquorice root, black tea, cinnamon and dry oak, while its
 lighter face had figs, guava, raspberry jam and fruit cake. Water brought sauna
 wood and clove-studded ham to the nose; cough syrup, rich toffee and Chupa
 Chups to the palate. After transferred this into a sherry butt for the remainder of its maturation.

JUICY, OAK & VANILLA
 LADY OF THE NIGHT
 We noted fruity aromas of peaches, pears, and
 mangos at first. With time a perfumed floral scent
 took over which reminded some of a `lady of the
 night'. Hot and almost over-the-top sweet perfumed
flavours attacked the taste buds neat and only a dash
 of water released the pressure. Now a lot more
balanced, spicy tart with pepper sauce and star fruit,
polished conkers using beeswax and in the taste, pu
pastry with cinnamon sugar and Bourbon glaze. After
 this whisky directly into a Sauternes cask for the
 remainder of its maturation.

"Eve`s Pudding with Cr�me Patisserie"
One of only three operating Lowland
distilleries, this one overlooks the
Clyde near Bowling. This cask was filled
by the Society in 1990, and it has done a
good job. The 
first impression is quite prickly, with some
soft heather notes, but these soon blow off to
be replaced by cr�me patisserie (like creamy
custard), iced caramels, vanilla sponge, Leb-
kuchen biscuits and (the key-note) Eve's ap-
ple pudding (i.e. apple sponge). Some also
noted elderflower cordial. Water brings
up fresh oven baking notes for a moment,
then the apple sponge returns. It is also
apparent in the flavour, which is at once
soft in the mouth and prickly on the
tongue. It takes a lot of water, and the pri-
mary taste is sweet and oaky.

Highlands, Speyside (Deveron)
 Lychees and Rumtopf
Built in 1962 and now owned by Bacardi Mar-
tini, this distillery takes its name from a fishing
village on the banks the Deveron estuary. Dis-
tillery bottlings bare the name of the estuary
rather than the distillery. Produced only after opening, this sample has had plenty of
time to develop a deep amber hue from its refill
hogshead home. First a warning: this "old man"
may seem butch and bold at first, but adding
water exposes his frailty. The Panel recom-
mends drinking this dram neat. On the nose we
savoured rich and fruity aromas of Rumtopf
and digestive biscuits balanced with fresher
hints of kiwi and Chinese lanterns. The flavour
at first shouted "lychees, lychees and more ly-
chees!" then developed with orange pith and
red cola-cube sweets. A light oily mouthfeel
(like eating black olives) guaranteed a long and
satisfying finish. Sit back and enjoy every sip,
but spare the water!

Speyside, Lossie
 Hawaiian holidays
The nose was wonderfully juicy with Sau-
ternes, cola and rum soaked fruits in trifle
topped with maraschino cherries. A warm forest
of cedar and pine sap. To taste it was all red:
Big Red chewing gum, cherry cola, cinnamon
sticks and strawberry jam. The addition of wa-
ter was like a tropical rain storm. One astute
botanist observed the floral aromas of
plumeria and tuberose in a Hawaiian lei. `Beef
Hoola Hoops!' Honey glazed monkfish washed
down with Mai Tai's on the beach. The final
fling of the holiday was feet up, hippy pipe
tobacco and heavily waxed leather.

Speyside, Lossie
 Playing with 
To begin with all the aromas were white;
chocolate, pepper, marshmallows, vanilla ice
cream and natural yoghurt. Slowly 
added; lemon and lime, bananas, strawberries
as well as other fruits of the forest. The
taste was hot and peppery, white chilli choco-
late but at the same time sweet, fruity and
sour like Haribo Tangfastics � quite an experi-
ence. With water the fizziness of a cream soda
and carbonating fruits with dry ice appear
alongside the creaminess of a pineapple milk-
shake and a key lime pie. The taste changed
completely, extremely smooth like a dollop of
rum and raisin ice cream with a hint of cin-
namon.

Speyside, Lossie
 After church
A venerable library � polished wood, candles, hes-
sian tapestry � with a fruity complex behind
(over-ripe pears, bananas and pineapple). Then an
empty fireplace (cleaned out for the summer)
or dusty store, with dried marjoram. The waxy
notes increase with water (church candles, on
brass candlesticks), then tablet, vanilla fudge,
linseed oil and vegetable oil, `spice drawer' and
dried orange pomander. The taste, straight, is
sweet overall, with traces of scorched newspaper
in the finish, and a hint of cinnamon toast mid-
palate. Warming, with nutmeg and sandalwood
in the aftertaste. With water the taste is
more waxy; rich and sweet, with dried orange peel.
 
 
 Flavour profile: Sweet, fruity & mellow

product_name: SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
tasting_notes_raw:
SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
 C AS K N o. 7.1 0 5
 CRICKET PAVILIONS AND GARDEN CENTRES
 The interesting nose combined toffee, honey and butterscotch sweetness with
 various fruits (apple, lychee, lemon, pineapple) including dried fruits and nuts
 (tropical mix); evocative aromas of wood, leather, linseed oil, cut grass and gorse
 took us to cricket pavilions. Water brought out exotic fruits and pot-pourri in
 wooden bowls and garden centre impressions. The palate had lovely sharp fruity
 sweetness � like assorted Haribos � but more of an adult pleasure (sour apple,
 cherry, apricot) with hints of gingerbread, chestnut, vanilla and Madeira. A good
 long finish at full strength � with water, light tingles of pineapple cubes, cinnamon
 toast and American Cream Soda.

Speyside, Lossie
 Take the MilkyWay
On first sniff, bananas, peaches in syrup, or-
ange blossom and orange barley sugars.
Vanilla and juicy oak begged us to take a sip,
but not just yet. Cloudy lemonade fizz, spicy
wedding cake mix and creamy nougat sweet-
ness tempted further. "Wow!" went the taste.
Top quality American oak gave flavours of
lemon and sugar pancakes, Edinburgh rock, blue-
berry muffins, cherry bakewells and hot but-
tered malt loaf. Water stirred aromas of
white chocolate and raspberries. Intense vanilla,
frangipane and Juicy Fruit gum raised eye-
brows while someone was reminded of
holidays in Portugal with Past�is de Nata
(custard tarts). Cooling Softmints, Turkish
delight, MilkyWays and toasted coconut to
finish.

Speyside, Lossie
 Sweet melody - jazzy harmonics
 The nose trumpeted sweet notes (toffee, jam
 roly-poly and custard, vanilla, bubble gum;
 then crooned cherry blossom and pot-pourri � as
 an after-thought it whispered toasted coconut,
 raisins, sultanas, nuts and banana chips. It
 changed its tune slightly with water � fra-
 grant basmati rice, pencil shavings and Scalex-
 tric formed a curious jazz chord. The palate ran
 with the sweet baton � toffee, fudge, cara-
 mel, chocolate, vanilla ice-cream, cr�me br�l�e,
 Oreos and bourbon � just held back from over-
 sweetness by nutmeg, toasted oak and Camp
 coffee. With water, we warmed happily to its
 adult sweetness of dark chocolate Magnums, pe-
 can pie, sweet sherry and chocolate-coated cher-
 ries.
 
 
 Flavour profile: Juicy, oak & vanilla

OLD & DIGNIFIED
 C AS K N o. 7.1 1 6
 IT'S GOOD TO ARRIVE
 Utter silence, you could hear a pin drop at the first nosing and it took some time for
 us to come out of our trance before some aroma descriptors were muttered; rum
 soaked raisins, dates, figs, sultanas, walnuts, cinnamon, baked apples and ripe cherries.
 The taste neat was rich, sweet and smooth with exotic spices, charred oak and dark
 chocolate. Even more elegant with the slightest drop of water like vintage leather seats
 in an E-Type Jaguar with handmade Oriental rug car mats and unlit cigars lying on
 top of the wooden dashboard. Whoever said "to travel is better than to arrive" was
 wrong!

product_name: YO U N G & S P R I T E LY
tasting_notes_raw:
YO U N G & S P R I T E LY
 C AS K N o. 7.1 3 3
 A BAG OF BOILED SWEETS
 Very prickly to start, then develops into zingy boiled sweets � acid drops,
 lemon sherbets; fresh overall, but with an oaky base, especially apparent on
 the tongue. Water introduces canvas and plastic (new trainers), warm
 leatherette (the interior of a new Jaguar), the sweet freshness now sour green
 apples and travel sweets dusted with icing sugar. The taste is sweet, then
 immediately sour; spritely, with mulled wine spices and a warming finish. This
 would drink well straight from the freezer in a chilled martini glass.

"A Devine Spirit"
Sampling this whisky in the week that
Pope John Paul II died, the Panel
thought it was appropriate that its
name means "Place of the Holy Man".
This fine old sample from a sherry butt
has certainly been blessed with some
heavenly aromas. On the nose, it is ap-
ple strudel and polished mahogany fur-
niture. "Like a Bloomsbury library"
said one of the Panel. Our taste-buds
were treated to pudding cakes with
Demerara sugar and bitter almonds.
Some detected dark rum and banana
bread. Water is recommended and it
can take plenty changing subtly with
each drop added. The nose (with wa-
ter) hints at Caramac bars and to taste
a surprising note of BBQ spare ribs,
spiced tobacco and sour cream. Long
and smooth in the finish.

A private membership club
 
 "Just Amazing"
This distillery was built in 1894, four years
before its next-door neighbour Benriach. In
this orange mahogany offering from a
sherry butt, the cask has imprinted its DNA
but the lightness of a superb whisky shines
through. The neat nose has acres of fruit
(pineapple, prunes, raisins), bags of nuts
(almonds, Brazils), treacle toffee and some
sherry. The main themes continue with wa-
ter (mixed peel, Cadbury's Fruit and Nut,
Fruit Spangles) along with fudge and
roses. The flavour is full-bodied and spicy
(blackcurrant, treacle, liquorice, cloves,
dark chocolate and orange). Fantastically
rich, but wonderfully light and velvety
smooth � just amazing.

"Rich and Heady"
Ranked Top Class by blenders, this malt is
a key ingredient in the Chivas blends. The
distillery stands to the South of Elgin, and
was built on a former cell of a 'holy man' -
a fact which is reflected in its name, which
is Ancient British. This pale gold dram
took us to bourbon country with rum & rai-
sin, scented wood and dried coconut.
With water it's sweet but savoury - apple
strudel with a fudge topping. The taste is
outstandingly rich and heady. It has or-
ange and spicy cinnamon in the flavour.
The richness remains with water on the
palate, it has a great sweet lengthy finish.
This reeks of quality and would make a
great Autumnal dram.

"Church Pews and Tobacco"
Immediately the panel was taken by
this old style dram with aromas of
wood polish, rich thick honey and cof-
fee beans. The reduced nose was differ-
ent but just as impressive; there was
scented cedar wood, church pews and
tobacco. The taste is sweet (liquorice)
and tannic (French polish) with brown
sugar and mint. There is a brandy fin-
ish. With water the palate has a slight
smoky edge. Tobacco perhaps? There
are more rich and fruity notes balanced
with the tartness of a Fisherman's
Friend in the finish. It takes water ex-
tremely well.

Highlands, Speyside (Lossie)
 A lively, fruity complexity
 Fabulous ruby tints were reflected in the
 nose � pomegranates, blood oranges, black-
 currant jam, glac� cherries and Vimto. Lots
 of fruit and Demerara; someone said, "Nutty
 characters" the rest of us bristled. The pal-
 ate was tannic but fruity with pomegranate,
 bitter marmalade, vanilla, caramelised sugar
 and angostura; delivering a great afterglow. The
 reduced nose changed again � magic bal-
 loons, cough syrup, coal-tar soap, Ambre Solaire
 and nut oil. A drop of water elicited a lively,
 fruity complexity; the Whisky-bard remi-
 nisced about raspberry wafers and `monkey's
 blood' on ice-cream cones. A very special
 dram from the distillery built by John Duff
 in 1894.

Speyside, Lossie
 Elegant ladies taking tea
The nose was attractive and evocative � lady's
perfume (talc, Yardley) soft leather, raincoats,
mint, nettle, Plasticine and soap. In reduction,
fruits emerged (banana loaf, apple pie, pear,
berry compote, lollipops) with tea cakes,
chocolate and perfumed cigarettes � imagine
elegant ladies smoking after drinking tea.
The palate was absolutely fabulous! Big fruit
flavours (apple, raspberry, pomegranate)
swirled around with perfume, leather, oak,
coconut meringue and mint leaf to gain our re-
sounding approval. With water � elegant and
delightful � fruity perfumes, cookie jars, but-
terscotch, shoe shops and Woodbine fags on
an oak mantel-shelf. The founder of Nikka
had work experience here in 1919.

Speyside, Lossie
 Dapper Dan meets Holly Hunter
 Funny how old Speysides can start on the
 nose like paint before gliding effortlessly
 into sensual exotic fruits � this was like that �
 lemon, cherry, mango and jelly beans; also
 rich toffee, black jack chews, geranium and
 elderflower. The palate had refreshers, coffee,
 cocoa powder, orange liqueur, tobacco, Parma
 violets, perfume, leather and waxed jackets �
 somewhere between George Clooney's Dap-
 per Dan pomade and Holly Hunter's handbag.
 With water, the nose seemed even more
 perfumed � waxy pine needles and sage. The pal-
 ate's sweet fruitiness (cherry Bakewell tart) was
 complimented by espresso dregs and cinna-
 mon stick. This Chivas Bros distillery lies
 south of Elgin.

Speyside, Lossie
 A little dab'll do ya
Quite a nose prickle to start, green unripe
apples but then becoming warm and homely
like a comfort blanket; sweet, slightly
smoky, dried tobacco, barley sugar and a malted
milk hot chocolate. The taste neat had some-
thing best described as `old fashioned'; an-
tique chest of draws with dusty old maps
and thick leather bound books, coconut coffee
hobnobs and grandad's Brylcreem. Adding a
little water, `use more only if you dare`, a single
matchstick lighting a cigarette, an old well- worn
Tweed jacket and liquorice all sorts. The
taste reassuring and yet again comforting;
oaky, leather sofas and sweet smoke tobacco.
This sample comes from the distillery built
in 1893 on the site of a grain mill and an old
chapel.

Speyside, Lossie
 The Perfect Comfort Blanket
 The nose neat is very comforting; bread and
 butter pudding, plum crumble, dark chocolate
 with raspberries or bitter orange, caramelised
 sugar, an empty cigar box and freshly
 ground coffee. The taste did not disappoint;
 Peach Melba yoghurt with a sprinkling of white
 pepper as well as cinnamon and cardamom.
 Only a drop of water transported us into the
 kitchen for breakfast; fruit scones, brioche,
 toast, Golden syrup sponge cake, cocoa
 powder and fresh fruit salad. The taste is very
 moist like an apple sponge cake or a peach cob-
 bler with custard and vanilla ice cream.
 This is a classic example from the distillery
 that switched from direct coal firing to
 steam heating as late as 1994.

Speyside, Lossie
 A complex cornucopia
 The nose held almost everything � lemon-
 ade, sherbet, cake mix, buttery flapjacks, pink
 wafers, chocolate bourbons, light tobacco,
 leather satchels, honey, golden syrup, Deep
 Heat, root ginger, dunnage warehouses
 and forests after rain. The palate started sweet
 (chocolate chip cookies, sweetie cigarettes) be-
 fore developing heat (rich Jamaican ginger
 cake, chilli) finally lemon-scented air freshener
 and light woodiness. The reduced nose
 evoked an old-fashioned Steamie, with linens
 hung up; then delicate suggestions of iced
 lemon cakes and buttercup meadows and the
 inside of a new shoe. The palate now devel-
 oped Fry's Chocolate Cream and almond fingers.
 The distillery is next to Benriach.

Speyside, Lossie
 Silk Sarong Seduction
 Caramels swimming in the foam of a choco-
 late porter; apricot liqueur spilled on a ball-
 room floor; a leather purse, tanned with Bur-
 gundy and sultriness, left on a barstool.
 The mouth is a silk sarong of smuggled rum
 and toasted acorns held in the arms of a
 woman with perfume dabbed on her wrists. A
 little water gives us her mouth, shaped
 like a fresh fig, after she's washed down al-
 mond macaroons and orange fudge with cola
 gone flat on the site of an old chapel in El-
 gin. Finishing with betel nuts wrapped in hon-
 eyed firefly wings for sweetness and light.

Speyside, Lossie
 Cedar, sandalwood and cinnamon
 We found rich aromas of dark honey, vanilla,
 coconut, chocolate, menthol, abundant leather
 and the deep woodiness of a cooperage,
 but somehow the nose also drifted towards
 tropical fruits and garden impressions with
 fresh flowers and herbs. The neat palate tin-
 gled the tongue nicely with leather, orange
 zest, wood, green herbs and aniseed and ginger
 spice � sweet tobacco and floral perfumes
 kicked in to create a wonderfully balanced
 and rather sexy experience. Water brought
 cedar, sandalwood, cinnamon and candy floss to
 the nose and pleasant pot-pourri perfumes to
 the palate. An attractive offering from this
 Chivas distillery south of Elgin.

Speyside, Lossie
 Fresh, tingly fizz-bomb
 The nose began with a fresh, fizzy kick
 (sherbet straws, orange Cremola Foam,
 lemon zest, green grass, foamy strawberries,
 fresh-cut melon) but settled to bon-bons and
 biscotti before slowly edging towards tobacco
 and leather. The palate delivered a big, tingly
 fizz-bomb of grass and pear-drops with rich
 sweetness (dark chocolate, caramel wafers,
 Thornton's toffee) and good depth (tobacco,
 coconut, vanilla, leather). The reduced nose
 became gentler and sweeter (rice crispy cakes,
 pink wafers)while the palate developed blos-
 som honey, quinine, watermelon, white pep-
 per and marmalade on toast � juicy and per-
 fumed with a fine bitter-sweet balance. The
 distillery was founded by John Duff.

"Foxgloves and Spangles"
The distillery has the only Saladin malt-
ings on Speyside, which supplies its en-
tire requirement. It stands in a glen
within Knockando Parish and used to
have a visitor centre within a small ru-
ral railway station on what is now the
Speyside Way. Drawn from a butt
(refilled), giving the Whisky a uniquely
interesting effect. Yellow gold in 
with a first nose of Sauternes and or-
ange water, then a bunch of floral notes
� foxgloves, cowslips, pollen � and some
chocolate and toffee. The flavour at full
strength is surprisingly bitter and dry,
given the nose � a combination of bitter
chocolate and mead. Water brings up
tinned mixed fruit (pears and pineapple
especially), Spangles and white choco-
late drops covered in hundreds and
thousands. It has a silky full mouthfeel,
with white chocolate in front, raisins in
the middle and a bitter sweet chocolate
finish.

"Fruity"
Built on the site known locally as 'the smug-
glers glen' this was one of the first distilleries
to install a Saladin box for malting which is
still used to this day. Straw yellow from a refill
barrel, this is very fruity on the nose. Pear
drops and a hint of smoke are followed by
melon, paw paw and cantaloupe. Tasted neat
it fizzes on the tongue, the light fruits remain
as does the smoke. With water the fruitiness
becomes moist like a fruit loaf with butter on it
and the taste has a bit of spice. This fruity
simple dram takes time to open up and makes
a great aperitif.

"Fun Fair Food Stalls"
This distillery was built in 1840 in Rothes
and was the only distillery in the town for
the next forty years. When in the 1960's
they began to export their 5 year old to Italy
they broke new ground for the whisky in-
dustry. A 
there is a carnival of rich, intense notes
displaying the benefits of a good cask;
sweet toffee apples, caramel, farmhouse
sticky toffee pudding and green leaves.
This is followed by creaminess on the
palate, rather like clotted cream fudge,
more greenery and a rumour of chestnut
puree. Water releases the esters and al-
dehydes; fresh notes of apple blossom
and lilac. After time a little wisp of
smoke appears and rounds the nose off
nicely. The addition of water changes
the palate slightly to reveal a bittersweet
character with Caramac bars, twigs and
orange barley sugars. The panel were
reminded of childhood trips to fun fairs,
always asking for one more toffee apple.

Highlands, Speyside (Rothes)
 Nigella nibbling Pata Negra
First we were transported by the appearance.
No so much the 
oily, with pearly, lingering beads). The first
word on nosing was `voluptuous', and the first
sniff rushed us to an expensive deli: olives in
brine stuffed with Pimento, Bath Oliver bis-
cuits, thickly buttered and then � bliss! � Pata
Negra ham (the very expensive Spanish stuff,
from acorn-gorged pigs). The taste at natural
strength was sweet and smooth, with Camem-
bert cheese. Water raises poached pears with
tinned Carnation milk, and the taste is of
"creamy rice pudding, dusted with gold leaf
and ground ginger". Well done Major Grant!
 
 Cask : Age : Alcohol : 
 Date distilled : November 1984

Highlands, Speyside (Rothes)
 Bringing in the harvest
 The nose was shy initially, but the general
 impression was of still autumn days; harvest-
 ing grass and cereals; various fruits in wicker
 baskets (apples, pears, plums). We also got
 boiled sweets (sherbet straws, fruit thins).
 The palate was fruity too, but ginger, pepper
 and tobacco gave it weight; the after-taste
 was quite distinctive (floral perfume, pine
 resin, sandalwood). The reduced nose had a
 life-affirming aromatic air about it; apple blos-
 som, laurel hedge and powder puff, with
 lemon citrus later. The palate, in reduction,
 seemed softer, more sophisticated with a but-
 tery glow and gentle heat. This Rothes dis-
 tillery has fine gardens.

Highlands, Speyside (Rothes)
 Garden in the Glen
The unexpected nose said `surprise!' with
the rich weighty sweetness of Sauternes
fruits (honey, banana, peachy and sugar), brioche
and marzipan. Millionaire shortbread brought a
traditional bakery alongside custard dough-
nuts, cookie dough and runny honey. The neat
palate revealed a subtle explosion; "malty
gold dust" said the Leither. Sweet and sour,
the taste was feisty with rhubarb and cus-
tard, candy floss, dried raspberries and Edinburgh
rock - "all the fun of the fair". Also Manzanilla
sherry and schezuan. The reduced nose be-
came fruitier and floral with elderflower and
cherry blossom. The reduced palate was warm
with hot chestnuts and German pan fried
roasted almonds coated with sugar. Pistachio ice
cream and cherry sauce lingered. This distill-
ery is renowned for its beautiful Victorian
garden.

Highlands, Speyside (Rothes)
Jam making and harvested fields
The nose was buttery (buttered toast,
croissants, bread and butter pudding) with
raisins, baked apples, custard, new-made
jam and mixed spice. The unreduced pal-
ate was big and full-bodied with lasting
heat � the flavours included intense fruit
and vanilla, poached pears with soft cinna-
mon spice and syrup and slightly burnt
pastries with currants. Water accentuated
the jam tarts (with icing sugar) on the nose
and introduced an earthy note. The reduced
palate, still rich and substantial, evoked a
jam maker's kitchen, fresh sourdough
bread and the comforting glow of autumn
sunshine on harvested fields. From the first
distillery established in Rothes.

Speyside, Spey
Mouth-wateringly sharp and sweet
The nose started out really fresh � laundry
flapping on the line, lemon, pineapple, straw-
berry and polished wood, but changed to cara-
mel, toffee and cinnamon; then later, to
leather and musk. The palate was spicy, oaky
and astringent � suggesting chilli heat or
spicy boiled sweets (aniseed balls, clove
balls). The reduced nose offered soft spice,
butterscotch, some wood shavings and plas-
ticine (`a carpenter's workshop') with
lemon spikiness. The reduced palate became
mouth-wateringly sharp and sweet (like Mof-
fat toffees) but also had little flickering flames of
gentle drying spice � Fisherman's Friends, cin-
namon. The distillery has a secret dram
safe in the gardens.

Speyside, Spey
 Melo-dram-atic
The fragrant nose wafted Murray Mints, Black-
pool rock, leather, apple, dark chocolate, gin-
gerbread people with currant eyes and a man's
shaving cupboard. With water it became a
fruity dessert served in an actor's dressing room
(sweat, hot light, dust, grease paint re-
mover). The palate, however, was sweet
and perfumed � with woody, spicy, men's co-
logne (the actor now freshly shaven); finish-
ing slightly nippy and drying with cold black
tea tannins. The reduced palate had cherry
lips and Juicy Fruit chewing gum; sweet, spicy,
playful warmth (was that actor Kevin Spicy?)
mingled with serious pleasure. Distillery
founded by the Grants (not Cary).

Speyside, Spey
Turkish delight and fragrant Thai rice
 The nose was attractively complex � green ap-
 ple, kiwi, peach and lemon zest freshness; al-
 mond slice, Turkish delight, apricot Danish
 and toffee sweetness; then floral dimen-
 sions in old roses, geranium leaf, straw, Medi-
 terranean herbs and fragrant Thai rice
 (jasmine). The palate offered toffee, jelly
 beans and dates, but blackcurrant and liquo-
 rice boiled sweets, cinnamon and Pernod
 provided deeper interest. With water, the pal-
 ate gave hints of smoke and ash, but
 mainly cooked fruits � apple strudel, rhubarb
 crumble, poached pear and baked apple with
 raisins. The palate was now a triumphant
 balance of tart and sweet. The distillery has
 nicer gardens than any.

Speyside, Spey
 Thai Noodle Stir-fry
The nose neat started off with a solvent
note (turpentine and nail polish remover)
but was very soon replaced by fresh and
fruity aromas of green apples, ripe bananas,
pear cider and Thai sesame noodles. Hot, pep-
pery and a ginger spice on the initial taste fol-
lowed by the bitter flavouring of tonic water
and finishing with the sweetness of cooked
bananas or stewed apples. With water, freshly
cut flowers in a vase in a kitchen whilst a
crispy beef stir-fry with lemon grass and spring
onions is being prepared. The taste is now
fresh and juicy like homemade ginger beer
and in the finish an old fashioned Bitter
Lemon.

Speyside, Spey
 Out of Africa
 Some of us were transported back in time
 into an African hunting lodge of the 19th century
 filled with mahogany furniture, a collection
 of trophies, antique rifles and their fine
 leather scabbards hanging on the walls and an
 overall scent of freshly polished wooden floor
 boards. In the taste sweet dried tropical
 fruits, fresh strawberries covered in icing
 sugar and madeleine cakes prepared with
 finely ground almonds and lemon zest. With
 the slightest drop of water initially a smell
 of cleaning the silver cutlery is soon replaced
 by brown sugar caramelized pecan and cashew
 nuts. In the taste the overall impression is
 fruity like a pear juice or a succulent honey
 sweet flavoured Medjool date.

Speyside, Spey
 White Chilli Chocolate
 Sweet notes dominate the aromas neat;
 brown sugar, golden syrup, toffee and the
 cream of coconut in a pina colada. With time
 notes of gingerbread and freshly picked
 blackcurrants appear. The taste has a devil-
 ish combination; just when a burst of fiery heat
 explodes in your mouth you get the creamy
 sweet sensation of white chocolate � quite an
 experience. With water fresh, grassy and
 herbal notes on the nose and creamy on the
 palate, like a white chocolate lime mousse or a
 white Russian flavoured coffee with an after
 dinner mint. Enjoy experimenting adding wa-
 ter to this exciting example from the best-
 selling malt whisky in Italy.

Speyside, Spey
 Quiet Time Dram
At cask strength the panel experienced a
light melody as calm waves of violin bow resin
and church pews reached noses. Scents of
sesame snaps and toffee apples increased
a sense of calm. On the tongue a bitter sweet
sensation as vanilla pod and cinnamon spice
combined with ginger and rye. The addi-
tion of water introduced savoury aromas
such as; pipe tobacco smoked in a rose-
wood pipe and balsamic vinegar soaked
bread. A substantial taste increased our ap-
petite for exploration as bracken and pine
nuts transported us to a bog-land setting.

Speyside, Spey
 Playing `Sea Battle' in the garden
 One Panel member found himself on the
 gun deck of an old wood-hulled warship with
 smells of ash, gun powder and spent cartridge,
 whilst others, more peacefully, are turning
 earth in their herb garden. The taste is hot and
 fiery � the battleship is in action � or we take
 a break from gardening on a sunny after-
 noon and enjoy rye bread dipped in olive oil. With
 water we take a rest sitting in a wicker
 chair on a warm cedar decking surrounded by
 pots of sage and heather. The taste now juicy,
 warm and pleasant like waffles with runny va-
 nilla custard.

Islay, North Shore
 Barbequed haggis
The first impression is not too impressive:
solvent, washing up liquid and Coal Tar soap; dried
meat, smoked mackerel and charred fish skin, but a
pleasant taste of boiled sweets and runny honey
on burnt toast, with a trace of fennel and rose-
mary in the finish and `the burnt end of over-
done roast beef'. With water the aroma is of
dried out haggis, and some allspice: dry overall.
The taste is still sweet, then burnt and slightly
peppery. Still some haggis, with a thyme-like
herbal note and charcoal in the finish. This dis-
tillery on the Sound of Islay usually makes
un-peated malt.

Islay
 Duelling banjos dram
 The unreduced nose had a definite kick -
 burning driftwood by boat sheds, canvas
 and leather (like a straight-jacket) and sucking
 salty smoke over oyster shells in a hookah
 pipe; but this duelling banjos dram had a
 pleasant side too � cranachan, honey, pear,
 citrus and vanilla; lime pickle and coal-dust
 never far away. The palate offered big, sweet,
 nutty smoke, liquorice, toffee and dark choco-
 late � grungy for sure, but tastier than ex-
 pected � fruity flavours swirling around in a
 briny, oily puddle and chipotle and Tabasco tin-
 gling away at the mouth, like a memory of
 combat. The distillery is near a wreck.

Islay
 Beware of the monster
A fruity and meaty nose initially with wine
gums and honey glazed ham. Earthy notes are
found alongside aniseed, fried mackerel skins,
fabric elastoplast and germolene. Smoke is
present but be prepared as something
much bigger than anticipated is lurking...
As you take your first sip the full wrath of
this peat monster is unleashed, singeing the
tongue with hot charcoal and lavender ash.
This adolescent beast can be tamed by
adding water, bringing out heather, gorse
and a light soapiness but the meaty notes -
now mussels and spare ribs are long-lasting.
Salty and ashy with soy sauce on the palate
from this usually mild Islay malt.

product_name: O I LY & C OA S TA L
tasting_notes_raw:
O I LY & C OA S TA L
 SEA SALT CARAMEL ICE CREAM
 A fresh, maritime and `seafoody' aroma greeted the Panel. A plate of cold
 smoked salmon, steamed mussels, crab claws, jumbo king prawns and fresh
 oysters with a sweet citrus soy sauce; whilst the freshness was in the desert;
 mint chocolate chip ice cream. The taste was like a salty, juicy gammon steak
 with a lime ginger salsa and sweet peat smoked mackerels. With water we
 moved into a fishmonger's with ice filled boxes on the floor containing the
 catch of the day and to taste a balance of sweet, salty and smoky flavours �
 dark chocolate mousse centred with smoked sea salt caramel.

DEEP, RICH & DRIED FRUITS
 LIVE LIFE ON THE EDGE!
 From the word go it became clear this was no ordinary dram. Imagine yourself
 opening a box of brand new leather riding boots, or squeezing a tube of double
 concentrate tomato puree or drinking a hot steaming mug of Bovril to which you
 have added Maggi seasoning sauce. The taste was sweet, thick and comforting like a
 steamed treacle sponge pudding and sherry soaked raisins in an almond cake. Adding
 water, and we were horse-riding across an empty beach on the Costa de la Luz during
 a short sharp shower and we ended up eating bacon-wrapped dates with a glass of
 Amontillado.

product_name: YO U N G & S P R I T E LY
tasting_notes_raw:
YO U N G & S P R I T E LY
 SEA BREEZES OVER THE VERNAL MACHAIR
 The nose had vanilla ice-cream, apple, honey and milk chews, but what caught our
 attention were floral fragrances of heather, lavender and elderflower, gardens after rain
 and sea breezes over the vernal machair. The neat taste was intense, sharp and mouth-
 drawing, but clean � with flavours of light smoke, lots of citrus, rock-pools and parma
 violets � nice! The reduced nose ranged from sherbet straws to salted sweet potato
 fries � but the landscape evoked was gentle smoke drifting over the machair (thyme,
 bog myrtle, wild flowers) and sun on granite outcrops. The palate was lovely, fresh and
 sharp � smoke, salt, apple and lime.

P E AT E D
 AN OLD TAR
Once you get past the nose-prickle, the scent is reminiscent of the rubber-bands
inside a golf ball but quickly becomes medicinal (Germoline cream), with tinned fruit
cocktail, waxed jacket and lactic cows. The taste starts sweet and finishes like bitter
Colombian coffee, with `a warm hot water bottle' in the middle and coal dust in the
aftertaste. Water increases the water-bottle note slightly, then introduces Bavarian
smoked cheese, smoked sausage and synthetic ham wrapped in linen, with lingering
coal dust. The taste is very sweet, lightly salty and vinegary, with smoked dulse and
sweetened hot milk, finishing with `Finnish Tar Syrup'

P E AT E D
 D R I F T I N G AWAY
 Whilst beachcombing we came across tarry driftwood, plastic bags, devil's
 toenails (fossilised oyster shells), kiwis (the fruit, not animals or people!) as
 well as a scallop shell midden. Always with us in the air was a barbeque peat
 smoke which we eventually found, joining the group having dinner. Apple-
 glazed ham, king prawn skewers with honey & garlic as well as a shellfish
 salad with lime dressing. With a drop of water, as the sun sunk into the
 sparkling sea, we all drifted away wave after wave, one starting to paint a boat
 sailing on the horizon whilst another wrote a poem.

PEATED
 SMOKED GINGER
 PEAR BELLINI
 A very clean nose right from the start with aromas
 of white rye and whole wheat sourdough bread
slightly toasted with salted butter, and porridge with
 slightly smoky chestnut honey. On the palate there
was plenty of sweet smoke and ash, balanced by the
 lingering spiciness of caraway seeds and ginger.
 Adding water, spiced vanilla cookies and
 fruity/yeasty aromatic notes of a Ginger Pear Bellini
 traditionally prepared with Champagne and pureed
 peaches. Less ashy with more sweet flavours
 appearing, a sweet and spicy dessert with
 strawberries and peaches marinated in balsamic
 vinegar marinade and grilled in foil served over
 Greek yoghurt.

product_name: J U I C Y, OA K & VA N I L L A
tasting_notes_raw:
J U I C Y, OA K & VA N I L L A
 TRIP TO A SHOPPING MALL
 On the nose, lemon, elderflower and tinned fruit salad gradually gave way to deeper
 notes of cashews, raisins, cinnamon, ginger and Buttercup cough mix. The neat palate
 had light spice and lots of sweetness (marshmallows, cherry lips, cola cubes, foamy
 bananas, Nutella and sticky toffee pudding). The reduced nose offered banana liqueur,
 red laces and rum and raisin ice-cream; some panellists were transported to a
 shopping mall (noodle bar, hairdresser and confectioner nearby). Oaky spice and
 vanilla began to show through on the reduced palate, along with butterscotch, banana
 chips, popcorn and toasted marshmallows � and a hint of Murray mints.

"Peat, Grass and Delicate Fruits"
This distillery has the largest capacity of
any in Scotland, and is owned by the
Japanese. This bourbon cask was filled
with experimental peated new make
spirit. A mid gold 
pression on the nose is of sweet pink ger-
molene, with cereal undertones
(flapjacks). Very interesting! With a lit-
tle time, solvents also develop alongside
grassy nettle soup aromas. The taste at
cask strength is sensational: full, sweet
and peaty. With water, it holds together
well, although the peatiness decreases a
touch to allow grassy notes to the fore.
With this comes some delicate fruits: ar-
tificial watermelon flavouring and a bit
of lemon. On the palate, the diluted taste
is more astringent, and has an enduring,
smoky aftertaste. A chewy, phenolic
dram that is simply fascinating. A must-
try for Islay fans, and a perfect dram to
fox your friends in a blind tasting.

"Floral Notes and Honey"
This enormous distillery is owned by the
Japanese, and despite being the largest,
does not operate on full capacity. This is
an exceptionally old example from a
hogshead, with an attractive gingery
gold 
rich honey, spicy wood and possibly
some strawberry. The taste is very dis-
tinctive, with honey again, more spice
and a toasty finish. With water, slightly
more floral notes come up
(honeysuckle?) alongside some definite
paint aromas. The taste also has some
honey in there, along with a woodiness
that betrays its age. Old enough to have
picked up many eccentric ways!

"Peaches and Apricot Jam"
This is a highly regarded Highland dis-
tillery near the Black Isle. An old bottle
has recently broken auction records.
This, more reasonably priced sample, is
bright apricot in 
fruity nose; peaches and apricot jam with
a toasted, biscuity note at the back. The
taste is minty(humbugs). Water brings
out the classic oiliness associated with
this distillery but it lightens quickly leav-
ing a light, grassy dram with hints of tof-
fee bon-bons. Overall, it is lighter than
its age would suggest but enjoyed by the
Panel.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 What a stoater!
 We analysed the nose with cool detach-
 ment; identifying sherry, Madeira, vanilla,
 honey, maple-cured bacon, cough mixture and
 egg custard; but the taste blew us away �
 "What a stoater!" exclaimed one panellist �
 "A helluva dram!" said another � intense fla-
 vours of dark toffee, custard flan with pepper
 and chilli nip and hints of salty liquorice. Wa-
 ter brought thick-cut marmalade, flowers and
 distant fireworks to the nose. The reduced
 palate was sweetly scrumptious, but with
 slight smoke and ash, spare ribs in honey
 mustard sauce and leather ("like biting off
 driving gloves"). A big impact dram from
 the Alness distillery with unusual stills.

SPICY & SWEET
 IT'S A KNOCKOUT
 This was not subtle to start with, in fact, it felt like one of Mike Tyson's unbelievable
 knockout punches and after being counted out we were helped back up on to our feet.
 As we slowly recovered we could smell the aromas from the ringside seats of toffee
 caramels, sweet and salty buttered popcorn and monkey peanuts. The taste was
 initially a spicy hot dog but then, sweeter flavours of strawberries with molasses sour
 cream sauce emerged. Water brought out boozy orange caramel pancakes with crispy
 bacon and in the finish, clootie dumplings with Drambuie custard � one for the real
 grown-ups!

Highlands, Eastern Highlands
 Barley sugars rolled in ash
The nose delivered dried fruits, treacle, dan-
delion and burdock, belly pork roasted with
brown sugar and much later salt and hot stones;
one panellist got a hint of soap. The unre-
duced palate had sweet tobacco, slightly burnt
buttered toast and dark barley sugars rolled in
ash; the after-taste was fairly spicy. The re-
duced nose had cr�me caramel, Hessian and
dark honey. The reduced palate was very
sweet but with a darker, drier, tannic edge �
lavender, fruity jam, sherry, sweet onion chutney
� eventually going back to an echo of the
roast pork. The old distillery cat could easily
match Mighty Mouse.

Highlands, Eastern Highlands
Leather armchairs and old wardrobes
 The nose was certainly savoury (salty bacon,
 roast parsnips, beef in red wine reduction)
 but also sweet (buttery croissants, marma-
 lade, toffee) with hints of coke embers, engine
 rooms, tobacco, struck match, floral notes
 and `old wardrobes'. The palate was rich
 and substantial, oozing unctuous sweetness, but
 with balancing spiciness � maple syrup, trea-
 cle and a Jamaican Christmas cake. The re-
 duced nose offered zesty citric peel, candied
 fruits, salty toffee, leather armchairs and cof-
 fee. The reduced palate was an amazing
 dessert, combining lemon meringue pie,
 sticky toffee pudding and icing sugar-dusted
 biscotti dipped in espresso. The distillery
 houses the Famous Grouse Experience.

.
 Highlands, Orkney
 Boiled sweets and grapefruit peel
Bubble-gum and vanilla sponge, with boiled
sweets (pear drops and lemon sherbets); apple &
elderflower cordial, white wine jelly; after a while a
light soapiness. Fresh and clean overall. The
taste is sweet, sharp and hot � grapefruit and
lemon peel; powdery, with a pinch of salt. The
scent of grapefruit skins increase at reduced
strength, and the other aromas remain in-
tact � vanilla, lemon sherbets, pear drops, washing
powder. The taste is now sweeter and more
salty, with light acidity and an aftertaste of
lemon bon-bons. A fresh young aperitif from
Orkney's second distillery.

Highland, Island
 Very fruity, very tasty
We found lots of good stuff on the nose �
honey, toffee, vanilla, Battenberg cake, vanilla
and a variety of fruits (pear, apple, tinned
pineapple, strawberry, three-fruit marmalade). We
also found tarragon, straw, putty, menthol,
brass and a stationery cupboard. The palate
was tasty � majoring on fruit (star-fruit, rhu-
barb, peach, pineapple) � but also with
gummi bears, soor plooms, some interesting
ginger spice and a salty note. The nose shifted
with water � oatcakes, tea caddies and pepper
� the centre-piece still a bowl of fruit, but now
sharper (gooseberry, lime). The palate be-
came even tastier � Moffat toffees and coke with
lime. Orkney's smaller distillery.

"A Farmer's Friend"
This rare offering is from the distillery built
near the port of Buckie, on the Moray Firth,
to replace an earlier one at the port of Cul-
len. After a long maturation of first fill sherry butt, the nose contains a va-
riety of farmyard smells and given time the
caramel and treacle comes through. The
taste is warm, melted brown sugar with
cream. With water the nosing is of the sher-
ry, nutmeg and lemon rind. The reduced
taste is of a sugar topped cr�me Brule. This
dram is definitely for, but not exclusively for
the sherry lovers.

product_name: Seaweed, Soap and a Bracing Breeze
tasting_notes_raw:
"Seaweed, Soap and a Bracing Breeze"
We have often noted maritime scents in
this malt, which may (or may not) come
from its maker's situation not far from
the Moray Firth at Portsoy. The distill-
ery was built by local businessmen in
the 1870's, but has had a chequered ca-
reer and has been mothballed since
1986. This example comes from a hogs-
head and is the 
and presents a pleasantly scented nose,
with bath salts, shampoo and lavender
emerging after a dried or candied peel
start, with some cake mix and soft
fudge. It is with water that it begins to
reveal itself: as refreshing as a brisk
breeze blowing over a pebble beach,
with dried seaweed and seaweed soap,
and (what we have come to think of as a
keynote for this malt) pounded prawn-
shells in the development. The flavour
is pleasantly sweet and malty to start,
then acidic, with a trace of liquorice in
the finish.

Peaches and soft toffee
This closed distillery overlooks the Moray
Firth and was built around three mills. This
malt, rarely found as a single, was filled into
a -gold
years. The slow movement of the legs down
the glass is more indicative of its graceful
age. The initial nose is of peaches, soft tof-
fee, ozone and dusty barns. It is a full-
bodied whisky when neat, slightly hot and
drying but with no bitterness (again despite
its age). Water dampens things initially, so
give it time before it returns bright and
sharp. It is very easy to drink with water,
sweet then quickly drying. You'll find your-
self reaching for more.

"Cotton Candy and Lipstick"
Built around three mills over-looking
the Moray firth, the distillery is one of
those with a difficult name to pro-
nounce. Just as well that it is rare as a
single malt. This example is from a re-
fill hogshead and is light gold in 
The first impressions are of cotton can-
dy and lipstick. It is very lively in the
mouth at full strength, good balance,
vanilla custard and glycerine. Water
brings out red currants with a hint of
nail polish remover. Reduced, the taste
is very sweet with a hint of minty, va-
nilla tea.

"Apples and Grapefruit"
`The Edinburgh Malt', actually comes
from East Lothian and takes its name
from the ancestors of the English Opi-
um Eater. This example is mid-gold
(gamboge) in 
. The first impression
on the nose is `meaty' - roast lamb, per-
haps, or roasting tin, becoming sweeter
and more fruity (bruised pears), and
behind all this a hessian note. At full
strength the flavour is somewhat spicy.
Water changes it into `clean laundry in
an airing cupboard'; still a trace of
pears, a whiff of lemons. The flavour is
mouth cooling and crisp-we all thought
of grapefruit and Granny Smith apples.
The finish light and refreshing, an ex-
quisite Summer dram.

"A Lively Brunch Dram"
Now being referred to as the
?Edinburgh Distillery' this classic Low-
land is found in the fertile plains of
East Lothian, and boasts its own bowl-
ing green. Almost two decades in a
hogshead has produced a buttery gold
immediately but soon creamy notes
and bright notes of lemon, lime and
grapefruit appear. This is followed by
a remarkable hint of smoke and a dis-
tinct minty nose. This carries through
to the taste without water which is
fresh, minty and slightly smoky, yet
cleansing. With water the smoke dis-
appears to be replaced by a lively,
sparkling dram that had the Panels'
lips tingling for ages. Truly remark-
able.

"Anytime, anywhere, any-why"
This distillery is surrounded by the
great barley lands of East Lothian and
draws water from the Lammermuir Hills.
It is typically considered to be an aperi-
tif style of whisky. This pale straw sam-
ple from a that. The initial nose has lemon, jas-
mine and green tea, straw bales, creamy
vanilla, crunchie bars and honey. Very
easy-drinking, even at full strength, it is
sweet and spicy with some aniseed and
liquorice notes. The reduced nose has
subtle floral notes, citrus and hubba
bubba gum. A light, pleasant dram for -
well, anytime, anywhere.

Lowlands, Eastern Lowlands
 Exotic tales of summer
Lovely beads ringed the glass. The nose
told us tales of summer � bright, fresh, airy
vistas of green apple, white melon, cranberry
and flowers, but also the deep, sunny, warm,
earthy aromas of vanilla, straw, oats and
honey-nut cornflakes. The palate was even
more impressive � sweet and juicy (Haribo
gummi bears and liquorice wheels with
light perfumed lychee). Water opened up the
nose nicely � exotic citrus and gooseberry
pie with the fragrance of a flower shop. Lemon
and a hint of pepper on the reduced palate
made it extremely easy to drink. The barley-
fields of East Lothian surround the distill-
ery.

Lowlands, Eastern Lowlands
 Bringing in the Barley
Our first thoughts were of combine harvest-
ers in golden fields of barley; sweet bails of
hay, husk, meadow blossom and hessian
sacks of grain. Then buttery short crust
pastry, roasted chestnuts, sweet mince-
meat pies and Manzanilla sherry, with rai-
sins in a Waldorf salad. The neat palate
was almost hoppy, reminiscent of a real
ale IPA. The reduced nose was floral and
gristy, like barley through the mill; a muesli
mixture of husk and flour with nuts, raisins,
papaya and dried apricots. The reduced
palate was creamy with soy milk and bran
flakes, muesli and beer. This Lowland
whisky is brewed and distilled in the Lo-
thians, also known as The Edinburgh Malt.

"Laundry, Violets & a Cinnamon Spiciness"
This distillery re-opened recently under
the stewardship of Jim McEwan, and
they now produce three separate spirits
of progressive peatiness from the same
stills. This example is peated at levels
of the traditional whisky from this dis-
tillery, which is very lightly peated. It
is from a hogshead, and pale in 
The first nose is fresh and sandy, but
also slightly floral with a dry finish on
the palate. Add water and a scented
soap character comes up, and we swith-
ered between violet and lavender. This
soapy, waxiness also carries through
into the flavour, which has a slight cin-
namon spiciness also, Fairly typical and
a good aperitif for the Islay fan.

"Something of the Night"
This distillery is currently the only one
to grace the Rhinns of Islay. From a
of Pinot Grigio. The neat nose seems
young and evocative but changeable.
One Panel member thought of pine for-
est at night and another remembered
mountain bothy nights (wool, leather
and old wood). There is also some
scented soap, salt and rhubarb rock.
The neat taste is lovely m�lange of Ma-
deira sponge and Battenberg cake. Wa-
ter turns the 
becomes light and delicately teasing
while the taste is dominated by fruity
boiled sweets and slight saltiness.
Wonderfully complex.

Islay, Loch Indaal
 A feisty tongue-fizzer
Evidence of the quality of whisky since this dis-
tillery re-opened in 2001; the nose was not
vastly complex, but pleasant, with lemon puffs
and green apple freshness sitting along-side
buttery fudge and jam doughnuts. The unre-
duced palate had feisty, tongue-zapping fizz,
with apple snow, buttery notes and subtle
smoke. The reduced nose had the lovely sweet-
ness of apple pie and custard; later suggesting
eucalyptus. The palate retained all that vanilla
sweetness, balanced by hints of smoke and
some light bitterness (green wood, lemon zest
and sherbet). We thought this spritzy, aperitif
dram from the Rinns was stunning for its age.
 
 Cask : Age : Alcohol : 
 Date distilled : July 2002

Islay, Loch Indaal
 Islay twinned with Algarve
 The nose whispered delicate perfumes
 (buttercups, snowdrops, spring flower mead-
 ows above sea cliffs); also coconut, cream
 soda and McVitie's Gold Bars. Even in re-
 duction we found this nose sexily seductive,
 with sweet tobacco, sherbet straws, vanilla
 and mimosa flowers nodding in the warm
 breeze � like a twinning of the Islay and Al-
 garve landscapes! The unreduced palate
 had delicious sweet heat � Berwick Cockles
 and white chocolate with pink peppercorns �
 we also found heather flowers, bog myrtle,
 seaweed and white peach. With water it de-
 veloped Parma ham and leather, salt, smoke,
 wood sap and Chablis. This distillery's name
 means `the brae on the shore' in Gaelic.

Islay, Loch Indaal
 Campfire by sea cliffs
The nose had herbal notes (witch hazel,
eucalyptus, bog myrtle) intimations of sea cliffs
and then walnuts, peppered olive oil, bil-
tong, toffee and ladies' handbags (leather, nail
varnish, parma violets, maybe cigarette pack-
ets). The taste was huge � peat smoke, engine
oil, smoked ham, dark chocolate, toffee bon-
bons and somehow both salty and chalky. The
reduced nose found syrup, mango skins,
tarred ropes and a pine forest by the sea. The
reduced palate was still minerally (licking a
limestone cave), with star anise, red pepper-
corns and a campfire among the ferns � very cu-
rious indeed! From the biggest distillery on
the Rinns.

Islay
 A cheese-board in a surgery
This is a-typical of the regular whisky com-
ing from Islay's proudly independent distill-
ery, with the motto `The Dog's Bollocks' in
Gaelic: more phenolic. The first impression is
mineralic, with an acidic winey note, then a sharp
cheesiness (mature cheddar), with dried apricots
and fruit chutney, drifting into hand-made soap
and Vosene shampoo. At natural strength the
taste is smooth and sweet and slightly salty; pa-
prika-spicy in the finish and lightly medicinal in
the aftertaste. Water adds Elastoplast, but
also bicycle repair kit and trainers. Now the
taste is more maritime and salty, with some
toasted oats and sooty smoke in the aftertaste.

Islay, Loch Indaal
 A big, eye-watering slap
The nose forced shotgun shells and fire-
works on us � but also gave barley sugars,
custard and chocolate-coated foamy ba-
nanas; peppermint tea, liquorice, smoked
ham and old bonfires. The palate's big,
eye-watering; sherry slap took our breath
away � sweet red liquorice, cinder toffee,
cr�me br�l�e, treacle, cooked apples, ash
and peat. The reduced nose suggested bar-
becued lamb chops dripping on embers,
singed mint leaf and burnt lemon skin. Wa-
ter definitely improved the palate � now
sweeter (toasted coconut, vanilla, golden
syrup, raisins, cherries) � also woody
spices, crispy sage, and grilled lobster.
The distillery is on the road from Port Char-
lotte to Bridgend.

Islay
 The Vital Spark's engine room
Mineralic and nose-drying (a dry beach), then
scents of mouthwash, bandages, antiseptic
cream which increase in strength until
they become a full-blown First Aid kit, while
at the same time becoming sweeter, like
salt-water taffy. The taste, straight, is very dry
after a sweet and salty start, with a spicy finish.
Water introduces a grubby, old-fashioned
engine room (maritime, with exhaust fumes).
`Hard salt Swedish liquorice' was also
noted. The taste is now lightly sweet and
salty, with a whiff of holy smoke. From the
distillery which brought us `Yellow Sub-
marine'.

"Scented and Soporific"
This deep gold drop of nectar is
from a sherry butt. It was filled in
that renowned distillery which
overlooks the west bank of the
Spey near Telford's Bridge at
Craigellachie. The nose has cr�me
caramel, fig jam, marrons glaces,
burnt sugar, dark toffee and a bag
of Aberdeen butteries. With water
it is nutty and creamy, scented and
soporific, like vanilla dust sprin-
kled on a fire by an intoxicating
witch. But it is in the taste that the
big sherry hit arrives - burnt chest-
nuts, dates, roasting tins, lemon
zest, dark toffee and chocolate.
The finish is rich and mesmerizing.

"Succulent Raisin, Figs and Toffee"
This Craigellachie distillery has recently
opened a `story of oak' visitor attraction. A
sherry butt has given this sample a mahog-
any 
finds pear and vanilla cream soda morphing
into fragrant lipstick; raisins and figs, celery
and walnut and vanilla fudge. With water
there is baked apple, rum and raisin and
powder puffs in a lady's handbag. The unre-
duced palate is succulent, with toffee, or-
anges, mincemeat pies and maple syrup.
There is also some burnt wood and a linger-
ing finish. A drop of water (go easy) brings
out orange sponge pudding and spiced wood.

Highland, Northern
 Galactic root canal treatment
The nose started off spirity � white pepper,
new pine and varnish; then lemon candles,
lemon sherbet, liquorice, wood ash and old-
fashioned rucksacks (canvas and leather)on a
parquet floor � perhaps the start of a spring-
time excursion? Water calmed it down �
laundry, white chocolate, vanilla, milk bottle
sweets and pretzels. The neat palate was
definitely fierce � somewhere between den-
tal anaesthetic and Fireball XL5! � Scotch bonnet
chilli, lemon zest, glue and Haribo gums. It be-
came much sweeter in reduction � lemon
barley water, sweet and salty popcorn and St
Clement's cocktail � the heat now teasing
and playful rather than fierce. This distillery
replaced `Brora'.

product_name: SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
tasting_notes_raw:
SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
 POMANDERS IN A LADY'S PARLOUR
 The nose had undeniable sweetness (Edinburgh Rock, glazed fruit tarts in a
 patisserie and jam-making) but beyond that we found an enigma of teasing aromas,
 including Barbour jackets, scented candles, basketry, leather, polished wood, shale,
 sandalwood, fir and freesias. With water we detected more citrus and `rose creams
 and pomanders in a refined lady's parlour'. The palate was deliciously sweet and
 warming with a pleasant waxy mouth-feel; sweet flavours of marzipan petits fours,
 honey, Danish pastries, fruit fondants and chocolate truffles; but the experience
 made more complex with lemon, orange zest, leather, cinnamon, clove and aromatic
 oils. Brora's only working distillery.

Highland, Northern
 Bumblebees by the sea
The first aromas were predominantly dark
runny honey over crackers, followed by salted
lemon and fresh kiwi fruit. With time, cam-
phor and citronella candles burning in a damp
pine forest. Juicy Fruit gum emerged on the
nose and in the taste. It retained a white
peppery heat at full strength, with lemon
zest and lime posset emerging. Aspen bark,
cinnamon and spearmint all became easier to
find with water as if they had all been
washed up on a seashore. A muskiness
reminiscent of coastal dunnage warehouses be-
lied its age, but homemade lemonade and
green Starbursts lifted any hint of heaviness.

Highland, Northern
 `Say it with flowers'
The first impression is of sweet pastry �
shortbread � with vanilla notes, increasingly
supported by fruit cake or dried fruits steeped
in tea. In time it lightens: fresh figs, melon,
fresh grass, rosemary. At natural strength, the
taste is heavier: herbal tea and jasmine tea,
musty/waxy, nutty (macaroons, hazelnuts and al-
monds), flower honey. The last increases with a
dash of water, becoming more waxy/oily �
sunflower oil, cr�me Anglais, light nuts. Now the
texture is soft, the taste sweet with honeycomb,
then slightly bitter (edible flowers like nastur-
tiums) in the finish. Complex and ever-changing.
 
 
 Flavour profile: Sweet, fruity & mellow

LIGHT & DELICATE
 SILKY SMOOTH SUNDOWNER
 After a long period of silence, the first comment was
 `this is a whispering dram'. The aromas were very
 elegant, but one had to `listen' carefully and then it
revealed yellow gorse bushes on a cli side, vanilla &
Tonka bean scented candles and freshly crushed mint
 lemonade. The taste neat was grippy, teeth coating,
 like smoking vanilla and orange flavoured tobacco in
 a hookah. With a drop of water a lot more perfumed;
Tarocco orange, eucalyptus and sage hand cream and
 on the palate, as smooth as silk. After a Sauternes cask for the remainder of its maturation.

"A Surprising Explosion"
The original distillery in Brora was built
in 1819 and replaced nearby in 1968 by
the present distillery, which has the same
name. This polished gold dram from a
sniffling. The nose is enjoyable enough
with the chalky impression of an old la-
dy's powder compact, liquorice, hot-cross
buns, icing sugar and salt. The neat taste
however, is a surprising explosion of
warm flavours, salty, smoky and sweet all
at the same time. With water the nose
develops orange fondant or marmalade
and the taste holds up well. Smooth yet
vigorous, with spirited �lan.

"Oak, Smoke and Liquorice"
The name of this second most
northern mainland distillery is con-
fusing, since the original distillery
changed it and gave its name to the
new distillery next door. This ex-
ample has spent butt. It is oaky and smoke on the
nose with some pine needles. The
taste is dry, warm and floral with
lots of smoke. Water improves the
dram. It is sweet with liquorice and
sugared grapefruit on the nose. On
the palate, it's smoky with a hint of
orange oil and a lengthy, liquorice
aftertaste. This dram is wonderful
with water and ideal for allsorts.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 A bear hug from an old friend
 We all loved this dram; it inspired animated
 conversation and vivid impressions. The
 Whisky-bard was on a pier, eating chocolate
 and ice-cream. We became hungry for a ba-
 con and peppered smoked mackerel break-
 fast. The Lady-poet started talking oars and
 canvas bags but somehow ended up para-
 chuting, James Bond-style, onto a boat. We
 thought it an astonishing three-way balance
 of smoke (sweet pipe tobacco) salt and sweet-
 ness (vanilla fudge and Battenberg). The Malt-
 meister said it was "a bear hug from an old
 friend" and the Vault-master said, "It ticks
 all the boxes". The distillery was built in
 Brora in 1967.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 Sweet scallops in condensed milk
An intriguing multi-faceted nose: lemon and
honey, sweet scallops, condensed milk and scented
candles. Currant buns and grapes brought rich
fruitiness, whilst sea salt and sandy dune
beaches reminded us of the coastal loca-
tion. The taste was big and texture waxy,
like currant buns and honey in Greek yoghurt.
Sticky toffee pudding in condensed milk. With
water, the nose freshened, revealing rose
petals, lilies and violets. The Vault-Master
detected salted fudge and clotted cream, whilst
the Whisky-scientist found green flowers
with damp stems. The taste with water be-
came more typical, of sea salt and crushed
black pepper, waxy and maritime. The only
active distillery in Brora.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 Candlewax and red berries
At first this is solventy � marker pens and nail
varnish remover, with a trace of shoe polish
as a clue to what is to come, and a back-
ground of cake mix, vanilla, marshmallow and
glace cherries. The taste is sweet and waxy, with
a trace of scented smoke and Granny's raspberry
jam. The waxiness � a key-note of this malt �
rises magnificently with water, with old in-
cense, tangerine skin, boiled sweets, cranberries and
strawberries. Teeth-coating in the mouth; sweet
overall, but not cloying � enlivened by lime
sherbet and sea breeze. A classic example of
this distinguished malt from a distillery
which overlooks the North Sea.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 A Calming Silky Bath
A deeply indulgent nose with beeswax, thick
honey and linseed oil. Concentrated fruit des-
serts follow with plums and red cherries,
sticky toffee pudding and cooked banana in
warm sauce. The palate was rich too with
deep dark fruits (plums, cherries, blackcur-
rants), runny honey and powder puffs. The
reduced nose was elegant and refined �
waxed limes, blackberries and baked plum cake.
The reduced palate was wonderfully
smooth, creamy and waxy with cherry syrup
and chai tea. A lovely lingering fruity after-
taste. This Northern Highland distillery was
built by the Duke of Sutherland in 1819.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 Geologist's Dream
 The cooling Icelandic nose brought thoughts
 of tundra and sea with lemon splashed on dry
 stone; an empty beach with dew, grass and
 rock salt followed by fresh lime, balsam and
 pine resin. The neat palate was almost Chablis-
 like, licking lemon off flinty rocks or
 `sucking a pebble' said the tour guide. With
 water, the nose became clean with a sherbet-
 like fizz; washing powder on clean linen
 laundry drying on hot rocks; botanicals of juni-
 per, coriander and angelica brought depth. The
 reduced palate continued the effervescent
 theme with sherbet lemon, moondust, cremola
 foam and candy floss. This distillery has beau-
 tiful views over the North Sea and sources
 its water from the Clynemilton burn.

Highlands, Northern Highlands
 Moorland after rain
We immediately noted a lightly mentholated
effect, then a complex of fruity and woody
scents: artificial peach, fruit syrup, varnish, natu-
ral liquorice, stripped wood, sawdust, beeswax. The
taste, unreduced, is sweet, herbal and fruity
(`lime pith'), with light waxiness and white-
pepper spiciness. It takes a while to open up
with water, then becomes very fragrant
(patchouli and vanilla, meadowsweet and elder-
flower) and fruity (fruit salad chews, fresh pineapple,
rhubarb), with a whiff of snuffed candle. The
taste is sweet and waxy; the floral note is now
jasmine, and the fruity element Juicy Fruit chew-
ing gum and orange pith. The distillery stands
adjacent to another of the same name,
overlooking the North Sea.

Highland, Northern
 Massage in a Bottle
Initial essences of beeswax and guitar polish led
the panel down an extremely aromatic
path. Potpourri, scented candles and or-
ange oil tickled our olfactory senses, fresh
laundry (maybe towels) caused us to sink
into our seats. Lavender and orange blossom
emerged on the palate, coating the mouth
with a waxy chocolaty finish. Water height-
ened our spiritual experience as the room
filled with incense, hand cream, jasmine, pear
drops and ripe peaches. The flavour ex-
panded to encapsulate vanilla, white choco-
late and waves of oranges and watermelons.
We emerged from this dram relaxed and
sweetly sedate.

Highland, Northern
 Passion-fruit scented candles
Complex, warmly inviting � the nose envel-
oped us in fresh grass, sea breezes, lemon,
honey, white pepper, rosewater, jasmine
and `passion-fruit scented candles in a wooden
box'. The immediate taste had sweet, waxy,
lemony, citric flavours, but hot and slightly
bitter too, like star-fruit sprinkled with chilli. The
nose turned fruitier with water � stewed ap-
ple, candied fruits, boiled sweets and `banana
in a raincoat pocket'. The reduced palate
seemed sweeter, with candy canes, fruit
syrup, lemon meringue and sweet coconut;
still with its refreshing side � green twigs,
lime and aniseed tingles in the finish. The dis-
tillery name means `sloped garden'.

Highland, Northern
 An exotic tearoom experience
Lemon drizzle cake, dried pineapple cubes
and waxiness on the nose give way to fresh
ginger, gorse flowers and wood glue. Tasted
neat, there was a spicy pepper heat and the
waxy notes. The taste also offered peaches,
vanilla pods and an apricot cake. Adding wa-
ter led to notes of vanilla ice cream and tof-
fee sauce, lemon sorbet, spiced apple tea and
an indulgent orange spiced soap! The taste was
warming and exotic introducing Turkish de-
light, old fashioned perfume (lavender) and a
hint of ras el hanout spices. This cask
comes from the Brora distillery, whose
name means `sloped garden'.

Highland, Northern
 Hard glazed pretzel sticks
At first nosing very ashy, like a distant
erupted volcano, soon followed by various
lemon aromas; lemon oil, lemon zest and
lemon drizzle cake as well as a yeastiness of
rye sour dough. The taste neat initially fiery
like hot volcano ash but swiftly replaced by
sweet wood smoke. There is also an interesting
battle going on between the saltiness of
pork scratchings and the sweetness of a crystal-
lised orange. With water the nose turns fresher
like a sea breeze and fruitier with apricots,
pears and apples. This engaging sample
from the distillery situated in Brora, tastes
sweet like a bacon breakfast cake with maple
syrup but at the same time salty like a Sal-
zstange.

.
 Highland, Northern
 Rose petals on a tropical breeze
 The nose was a fresh, sweetly tropical breeze,
 carrying suggestions of lemon drizzle cake,
 lime, rose petals, toffee waffles, honey and vanilla;
 with white wine, grass, wood and wax all
 deepening the complexity. The neat palate had
 the mouth-nipping warmth of nutmeg and other
 woody spices, but was also fruity and juicy �
 lemon juice, Frutella, honey on toast, Demer-
 ara, shortbread and donuts � we were salivat-
 ing. The reduced nose continued perfumed and
 sweet � apricot Danish pastries, chocolate and
 polished wood. The palate now � so tasty � cin-
 namon-dusted cr�me br�l�e � gentle spices
 teasing and playing with perfumed, waxy fruits.
 From Diageo's most northerly distillery.

Highland, Northern
 Spritzy Citrus and Ikea Candles
The nose packed a punch of pink grapefruit,
fizzy sherbet, and cranberry followed by
delicate floral - citronella, lilac and elder-
flower. Tinned mango, wine gums and pista-
chio emerged, and hint of water butt on a
warm day. The taste was tingling and tropi-
cal with fresh wood, zesty mandarin and Edin-
burgh rock. Water delivered a box of Ikea
candles, Turkish Delight, lemon and ginger mar-
malade and roses after summer rain. The panel
were reminded of eating a meaty fish baked
in salt whilst sitting on a wet rock. A spritzy
finish softened with marshmallow, cream
soda and a handful of playdough.

Highland, Northern
 The Fisherman's Friend
 One of our panel members indulges in a
 spot of angling and instantly recognised
 the aromas of waxed jackets, wicker basket and
 oiled fishing reels. Crushed nettles and citronella can-
 dle, along with Autumnal orchards completed
 the riverbank scenario. The mouthfeel
 started with cooling starfruit and lemon drizzle
 cake, then slowly a honeycomb warmth
 crept over the tongue with stealth. Raisins
 plumped with cola, fruit salad sweeties and
 Black Jacks emerged when water was added,
 with some Springtime florals. A hint of flax-
 seed oil but overall deliciously juicy and distinctly
 moreish.

SPICY & SWEET
 HORSE HARNESSES AND MESCAL `WORMS'
 The neat nose was certainly varied � old books and cigar boxes in a study, horse
 harnesses, mescal `worms', a greengrocers shop and various savoury notes (smoked
 ribs, sausages, roast beef, onion chutney, salt and pepper cashews). Water improved it,
 finding the good spices from the excellent cask oak � cinnamon, anise, cumin, tobacco,
 treacle toffee and liquorice allsorts. The palate was rich with pleasant wood influence
 � black bun, incense smoke, barbecue embers, five-spice seasoning on pork crackling,
 mixed nuts and new leather. Water brought out the sweetness of Demerara, dark
 honey and teriyaki � bringing wonderful balance to this intriguing and unusual dram.

" Dried Japanese Seaweed in
 a Varnished Boat"
Voted 'best malt' by a panel of experts and
readers of Whisky Magazine, this mighty
whisky from Campbeltown's most famous
distillery consistently fetches high prices at
auction. This is a first-rate example of the
make. It comes from a re-fill hogshead and
is pale amber in 
time, with subtle waxiness and a sweetness
first like Hubba-Bubba bubblegum then like
brown sugar: the whole resolves as dried,
sweet seaweed. The flavour is sweet, with a
trace of light machine oil; quite peppery and
long. Water raises the oily note, and trans-
forms it to boat varnish � it is easy to con-
jure images of boat-yards, with marine
scents and fresh salt air (but no fish!). The
flavour is sweet and rounded, warming and
drying, with traces of fresh wood and a long
finish. An excellent dram, both straight and
reduced.

Highland, Southern
 Sweet, nutty personality
 Many years in cask had given the nose lin-
 seed oil, linoleum, waxed canvas, new car,
 sandalwood and allotment shed characters �
 but the darling barley seed bestowed the
 creamy sweetness of cr�me Anglaise and
 choux pastry chocolate �clairs; watermelon
 and pear completed the picture. The neat
 palate supplied the typical sweet and nutty per-
 sonality (the whisky, not the panel!) �
 Crunchy Nut cornflakes, peanut brittle ice-
 cream, hazelnuts, walnuts, muesli and di-
 gestive biscuits. With water, the nose found
 putty, macadamias, lemon curd and fruit cock-
 tail, while the palate became much more
 honeyed and we liked it better. The distillery
 is in Blackford village.

product_name: YO U N G & S P R I T E LY
tasting_notes_raw:
YO U N G & S P R I T E LY
 PILE-DRIVER PUNCH WHISKY
 The nose hinted at paint and glue � water shifted this to fresh linen and warm
 photocopies; we didn't find that in the taste. The rest of the nose had herbal, grassy
 notes (hay, thyme, cucumber) and fruity sweetness (brandy snaps, orange zest, peach
 stones, golden syrup, chilli marmalade). The palate had a pile-driver punch of spirity
 heat (even with water) but after a couple of sips we learned to take it on the chin �
 nice grassy, cereal notes, including popcorn, riverbank reeds and mint, then more of
 that fruity sweetness (mandarin, rhubarb and pineapple, with spun sugar, vanilla and
 pink Chewits).

product_name: SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
tasting_notes_raw:
SW E E T, F R U I T Y & M E L LOW
AUTUMN FEELINGS
This dram evoked autumnal feelings in us all, even though slightly different ones. From
walking in woodland searching for blackberries and mushrooms to grape harvesting
on a warm afternoon and picking apples in an orchard; eventually we all celebrated
harvest festival. For that we were eating plum, orange and almond cobbler, toffee
apples, caramelised pears and pumpkin pie. With water the first signs of winter
appeared, the cool wind and the comforting aromas of spiced hot apple cider and
vanilla scented candles drew us inside enjoying a cherry pie with a nutty crumb crust
and real whipped cream.

SPICY & SWEET
 PURE INDULGENCE
 This one made its presence known straight away. A
 rich and flavourful punch like dark thick cut Seville
 orange marmalade on spongy crumpets and black
currant jam sweetened with honey on buttered burnt
toast. The taste was that of seared duck breast with
 red wine and orange sauce. With water; cinnamon
 roasted pineapples and cinder to ee and the never
 ending finish was a dark chocolate cake flavoured
with Barolo Chinato and served with whipped cream
and raspberries � pure indulgence. After an ex-bourbon , we transferred this
 whisky directly into a Sauternes cask for the
 remainder of its maturation.

Islay
 Camping with M*A*S*H
Wow � the nose had so much � hessian,
canvas, leather, bandages, first aid boxes, sur-
gical soap, seashells, sea-weed, tar, bonfire
smoke � it was like M*A*S*H set up camp
on an Islay beach. The palate spoke confi-
dently of harbours and hospitals � lobster pots,
fish boxes, fishing boats, salted macadamias,
heather and mussels lined up against Big
Red gum, elastoplasts and sweet peat-smoke. Af-
ter reduction, the nose twitched at a breeze
